title_options: Popcorn Is A Pressure Vessel That Jumps (Physics) 🍿

share.myth: A popcorn kernel just explodes; there's no real physics in the jump or the sound.
share.truth: The kernel is a pressure vessel that fails at about 180 C; foaming starch forms a leg that is compressed on the pan like a spring and pushes the kernel off, and the pop is linked to escaping water vapour (Virot & Ponomarenko 2015).
share.line: Popcorn is a pressure vessel that fails at 180 degrees, then jumps on a spring made of starch.

facts: Virot & Ponomarenko 2015, J R Soc Interface 12:20141247: critical temperature 180 C consistent with a pressure vessel; popcorn jumps with a leg of starch compressed on the ground; pop sound linked to water vapour release; all within some hundredths of a second.
description: Popcorn is a lesson in pressure, stored energy and forces. The kernel is a pressure vessel, and it jumps on a leg of starch. #shorts #physics #science #popcorn
sources: Virot & Ponomarenko 2015, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12:20141247 (PMC4345489).

scenes.narration: A popcorn kernel is a tiny pressure vessel, and when it fails, it jumps.
The hard hull traps a little water inside.
Heating it turns that water into steam. Same space, more gas, hotter gas: the pressure rises.
The hull holds until about one hundred eighty degrees Celsius. Then almost every kernel bursts.
Starch foams out, and part of it lands on the pan as a leg.
The leg squashes, storing energy like a spring, then pushes the pan and the pan pushes back.
And the pop? Recordings link it to the steam escaping, all in a few hundredths of a second.
Popcorn is a pressure vessel that fails at one hundred eighty degrees, then jumps on a spring made of starch.
So what would happen to the pressure if the hull had a tiny hole?
